analysis.one_liner: Bans capturing, importing, exporting, or breeding orcas and similar whales for public display.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in August 2022, it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The SWIMS Act would have amended two existing animal-welfare laws to end the supply of captive orcas, beluga whales, false killer whales, and pilot whales for display. It would bar federal permits to capture or import these animals for shows, allow export only to sanctuaries or for release to the wild, and make breeding them for display illegal under the Animal Welfare Act. Animals already in tanks could stay, but no new ones could be produced or imported, so the practice would fade out over time. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: The captive whales themselves, by ending capture, import, and breeding for shows, which the bill's findings say conflicts with the animals' physical and social needs; and the public, which would no longer have federal law blessing confining these large-brained mammals in concrete tanks for entertainment. Marine mammal sanctuaries would gain a defined pathway for retiring animals. [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Bars NOAA from issuing permits to capture or import orcas, beluga whales, false killer whales, or pilot whales for public display.

Makes it unlawful to export these whales, except to a marine mammal sanctuary or for release to the wild, with a sanctuary defined as a non-profit refuge where animals are not used for display or breeding.
Makes it unlawful under the Animal Welfare Act to breed or artificially inseminate these species so their offspring can be used for public display.

Sets out Congress's findings that science increasingly shows these species suffer in captivity — premature death, repetitive stress behaviors, barren tanks — and states Congress's sense that they should not be held for public display.

analysis.who_pays: Marine theme parks and aquariums whose flagship exhibits rely on these whales. They could keep animals already in their tanks, but without breeding, capture, or imports their populations would age out and the core of the attraction would wind down. Communities and workers tied to those exhibits would eventually lose the draw. [S3]

drawbacks.text: Some in the aquarium and research world argue that public display funds conservation science and education, and that ending it removes a funding stream and a public connection to these species.

The bill leaves animals already in captivity in place; it does not require their retirement or release, only that no new whales be captured, imported, or bred for display, so conditions in existing tanks are unchanged by the bill itself.
Theme parks would keep existing animals and shows for years while populations age out, meaning a long, slow wind-down rather than an immediate change for the animals now held.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is humane and long-term: no new whales taken from the wild or born into tanks for entertainment, at the cost of a gradual decline in a profitable attraction for a handful of parks. The bill is narrowly drawn — it phases the practice out rather than seizing animals — but it does nothing for whales already in captivity beyond allowing export to sanctuaries. The stakes for most people are modest; this is an animal-welfare bill, not an economic one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in August 2022, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023, so no hearing, vote, or floor action ever happened.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the SWIMS Act on August 2, 2022, joined by six Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Under Senate practice, a bill dies at the end of a Congress unless it is refiled in a later one.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Marine theme parks and aquariums are better off because the bill died: current law still allows them to breed, capture, and import orcas and similar whales for their shows, so their supply of captive animals and the revenue that depends on it remain intact.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Senate Democrats and no opposition was ever recorded, because the bill never reached a hearing or a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill would let them keep whales already in their tanks and the shows those animals anchor, but it ends their supply: no breeding, capture, or imports for display, so the attraction ages out and their central revenue stream eventually winds down. Their financial interest runs against the bill's aim of ending confinement for display. [S2] [S3]
NOAA could no longer issue permits to capture or import orcas, belugas, false killer whales, or pilot whales for public display, cutting off the wild-to-tank supply chain. [S3]
Export of these whales would be legal only to a sanctuary or for release, creating the one lawful retirement pathway under the bill. [S3]
